core: The four pieces of a medical word — prefix, word root, suffix, and combining vowel — each defined and attributed
Prefix patterns: location (pre-, post-), number (bi-, tri-), and direction (supra-, infra-)
Root patterns: body parts (cardi-, gastr-, neur-, derm-, nephr-, hepat-, ot-, oste-) and functions/substances (glyc-, hem-, therm-)
Building a word: root + suffix, then prefix + root + suffix, with an original worked example
Reading unknown terms: spot the suffix first — the general practice, stated simply
The honest framing: word parts are a cheat code for the language, with clear limits
supporting: Combining form (root + combining vowel) as the unit that links into longer terms
Combining vowels drop out when the next part begins with a vowel (derma- + -itis = dermatitis; colo- + -ostomy = colostomy)
Recurrence: knowing a small number of parts helps interpret a large number of terms
The NLM tutorial groups suffixes by what they do (problems, procedures, specialties), which supports a suffix-first reading habit
outOfScope: The general definition of medical terminology as a field and the safety/precision argument (sibling topic: medical-terminology)
Anatomy and physiology depth (owned by the biology subject)
Clinical skills, assessment techniques, and documentation workflows (sibling topics)
Prescriptive spelling rules for constructing every possible term

claims.claim: Medical terms are built from word parts — prefix, word root, suffix, and combining form vowel — and a word root combined with a combining vowel forms a combining form.
The root of a medical word usually names a body part: bone is oste, muscle is myo, nerve is neur, skin is derm, heart is cardi, kidney is neph, liver is hepat, ear is ot.

Standard prefix meanings: pre- before/in front, post- behind/after, bi- two, tri- three, supra- above, infra- beneath/below, plus peri- around, intra- within, inter- between, uni- one, quadri- four, trans- across, circum- around.

Standard suffix meanings: -itis inflammation, -osis condition or disease, -emia blood condition, -algia pain, -ectomy removal/excision (removal by cutting), -otomy making a cut or incision, -ostomy/-stomy creating an opening.

The key to understanding an unfamiliar medical term is focusing on its components (prefixes, roots, and suffixes), and knowing the meaning of a small number of components helps with interpreting a large number of medical terms.

The NLM tutorial groups suffixes by what they do — problems such as -itis, -osis, -emia; procedures such as -ectomy, -otomy, -stomy; specialties such as -ology — which supports reading the suffix first to identify what kind of word a term is.
Combining vowels drop out when the next word part begins with a vowel — the NLM tutorial's own examples show derma- plus -itis becoming dermatitis and colo- plus -ostomy becoming colostomy.

Word-part decoding is an aid to interpretation, not a guarantee for every term: sources describe components as helping interpret many terms, and not all terms (names, modern coinages) decompose into standard parts.

positions: The NLM tutorial says -osis is 'condition or disease.'
Some other glossaries restrict -osis to abnormal conditions specifically.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the NLM wording ('a condition or disease') and does not claim a narrower clinical meaning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether -algia appears in all word-part lists.
positions: The Merck Manual glossary records 'alg' as pain.
The MedlinePlus appendix does not list -algia among its procedure/condition suffixes.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states -algia means pain, attributed to the Merck Manual, and uses it only in that meaning (arthralgia, joint pain).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'suffix first' is a sourced rule or a teaching strategy.
positions: Sources teach reading word parts generally without prescribing an order.
The NLM tutorial groups suffixes into categories, which makes the suffix the fastest way to identify what kind of term a word is.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents suffix-first reading as the lesson's own strategy built on the sources' category grouping, not as a quoted rule from any single source.

sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22: the tutorial landing page (page last updated March 6, 2020) and the full tutorial PDF (Tutorial_Understanding_Medical_Words.pdf, 25 pages). Supports: the root of a medical word is usually a body part (oste bone, myo muscle, neur nerve, derm skin; cardi heart, neph kidney, hepat liver); beginnings and endings (prefixes and suffixes) are added to roots to change meaning or add information; size, level/speed, location, procedure, problem, and specialty suffix groups (-itis inflammation, -osis condition or disease, -emia blood condition, -ectomy removal of, -otomy making a cut in, -stomy create an opening, -scopy viewing); worked combinations (derma- + -itis = dermatitis; colo- + -ostomy = colostomy; carditis, cardiology, cardiomyopathy, colitis, colectomy, colonoscopy). Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
